A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ensemble++ research. The complete 54-page v3 and 47-page v4, including appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables that can be aligned despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original linear and nonlinear bandit experiments, computational measurements, component ablations and GPT-2 hate-speech detection results.

after.justification: v4 reports original bandit evaluations, scaling experiments and language-model fine-tuning ablations, alongside retained empirical results.

M1.justification: v4 introduces a symmetrized cross-entropy objective for classification instead of squared loss (Appendix B, Eq. 19); v3 documents squared-loss training. The underlying linear updates, random ensemble combinations, fixed priors and stop-gradient architecture remain. Stop-gradient is retained in v4 Appendix B despite its reduced prominence in the main text.

E1.justification: The principal coverage remains: finite- and compact-action linear bandits, quadratic and vector-quadratic bandits, UCI Mushroom and Shuttle, and hate-speech detection. However, Neural Bandit changes from a continuous neural reward with Gaussian noise to a binary/Bernoulli reward task. Mushroom remains in v4's appendix despite disappearing from the main comparison.

E2.justification: v4 adds Greedy to nonlinear comparisons and directly compares Ensemble++ with linear Ensemble Sampling. Its documented EpiNet implementation adds raw inputs to the hidden-feature/index inputs described in v3 Appendix J. The bounded-update LMCTS comparison from v3 Figure 1 disappears, although the original LMCTS benchmark comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Neural Bandit's three-layer reward generator and additive Gaussian noise are replaced by a two-layer logit model with temperature 0.1 and Bernoulli sampling. v4 adds an explicit 0.02 normalized-regret criterion for matching TS, broader dimension sweeps, parameter-count trade-off evaluations, and frozen-versus-finetuned GPT-2/Pythia14m configurations. These introduce substantial new or revised evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: v4 removes v3's stop-gradient and OneHot/symmetrization ablations, independent-versus-shared-layer comparison, and shared-layer hyperparameter sweeps. It adds decision-set-size and regret/parameter-count analyses, expands distribution ablations, and introduces frozen-versus-finetuned language-model tests. The buffer-size analysis is retained and moved into the main text.

E5.justification: The reported nonlinear repetition count changes from five distinct seeds in v3 Appendix I.2 to ten in v4 Appendix F.2. Linear experiments retain 200 repetitions. Both versions display empirical uncertainty graphically; v4 does not introduce a clearly specified confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v4 replaces numerous nonlinear result curves and adds direct ES comparisons, scaling fits with R-squared values 0.98 and 0.93, parameter-count frontiers and fine-tuning results. The stated hate-speech advantage over Ensemble+ changes from 13.5% to 5%. Revised losses, settings and seed counts prevent treating these replacements as controlled cross-version performance changes.

T1.justification: The main covariance and regret bounds and most supporting proofs remain. v4 replaces v3 Appendix D's isotropic-update derivation with Section 3.2's ridge argument and explicitly excludes x0 = 0 in Theorem C.5. The new Eq. 6 omits fixed-prior contributions still used in Eqs. 7–9, introducing an inconsistency in the asserted equivalence.

C1.justification: v4 drops the headline emphasis on eliminating shared-layer coupling and sequential dependency, presenting its contributions as a small shared-factor linear sampler and a neural extension. The central claims of near-TS regret, logarithmic ensemble scaling and favorable empirical computational efficiency are largely retained.

C2.justification: v3's detailed gradient-interference and ensemble-homogenization explanation is removed. v4 explicitly acknowledges the absence of a nonlinear regret proof and explains its exclusion of EpiNet from text experiments. Appendix G adds interpretations about fine-tuning for evolving content and reduced moderator workload, although the reported publish/block experiment does not clearly substantiate the human-review interpretation.

D1.justification: v4 adds FIFO-buffer instructions, concrete EpiNet network widths and bias details, expanded parameter accounting, and hate-speech sample-count and labeling-threshold information. Conversely, v3's explicit default M = 8 and buffer size 50,000 disclosures disappear. The advertised Ensemble++ code location changes from a GitHub repository to an anonymous codebase.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially recast around scalable posterior approximation and ensemble-size requirements. v4 adds discussion and citations covering Laplace/variational inference, ensemble Kalman filters, Bayesian bootstrap, Hypermodels and additional EpiNet work, while removing several application-oriented references. The positioning shifts away from shared-layer coupling toward the computational-statistical gap in approximate TS.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, background, methods, conclusion and moderation discussion are extensively rewritten. The exposition now introduces the linear sampler before its neural extension. Former related-work, dependency and EpiNet appendices are consolidated, other appendices are reorganized, and the appendix contents pages are removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Opening runtime/regret plots are replaced by parameter-count frontiers; architecture and coupling illustrations disappear; new linear-scaling and fine-tuning figures appear. The buffer plot is relocated, and the minimum-ensemble table is replaced by expanded scaling plots. Many appendix distribution figures remain recognizable.

improvement.justification: v4 offers a clearer linear-first account, useful ES/Greedy comparisons, additional scaling and fine-tuning controls, and more nonlinear seeds. However, it removes component diagnostics and runtime measurements. New supporting arguments contain inconsistencies: Eqs. 6–9 disagree on prior handling, Appendix A.7.1 counts M+C outputs after specifying M×C, and Appendix G claims approximately 80% fewer human reviews without a matching evaluation protocol. These substantive gains and weaknesses prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
